messages.subject: Inactivity GGIR
parts:
Hello fellow GGIR community, 

I am a doctoral student at the University of Paul Valery in Montpellier, France. I am working on my last thesis article where I am investigating associations between physical activity and fatigue in people with schizophrenia compared to non-clinical controls.
I used AXIVITY accelerometers to measure PA and analysed the data using the GGIR package.

I am wondering if there is a way to measure SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR - and not just inactivity? I have read through the GGIR data processing document, but do not seem to find any mention of sedentary behaviour.

Would someone please let me know if there is an independent measure of sedentary behaviour?

Thank you for your help.

Kind regards,
Yasmine Laraki

messages.author: 5270e62a7d3ec577
messages.subject: Re: Inactivity GGIR
parts:
Hi Yasmine,

According to the widely accepted definition of sedentary behaviour (See table 5, Tremblay et al, https://ijbnpa.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12966-017-0525-8#ref-CR25), it is done in a "sitting, reclining or lying posture". I'm assuming your participants wore the Axivity on the wrist, therefore there will be no way of determining what posture the participant is in - therefore the terminology is inactive time from GGIR because some of that inactive time likely includes behaviours such as standing.  

Though there will be a large crossover between inactive and sedentary time, the terminology is important as the 2 behaviours are different, particularly from the perspective of a sedentary behaviour researcher - hence why monitors are generally worn on the thigh where sedentary behaviour is of particular interest (e.g. Axivity on the thigh as done in ProPASS, and the activPAL worn on the thigh).

Thanks, 
Ben

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: Inactivity GGIR
parts:
Hi Yasmine,

In addition to Ben's response: Keep in mind that these definitions of sedentary behaviour are only words. What matters most is whether the methods we use truly capture the behaviour these words describe.

In my personal opinion "sedentary behaviour" has been defined in an unfeasible way. Some methods such as thigh worn sensors may be good at capturing the sitting/reclining aspect of it but it is questionable whether those methods can capture the <1.5 MET criteria consistently in the real world as humans can work with their arms that involves more than 1.5 MET of energy expenditure while sitting. Also thigh worn data has the major flow that it is not good at distinguishing sleep as the posture is identical to sitting on a chair for a while. Similarly, other methods such as wrist or hip worn sensors may be good at capturing the 1.5 MET-criteria but fail at capturing the posture criteria.

So, for that reason I have tried to avoid using the term "sedentary behaviour" in the GGIR documentation. Although, maybe it is good to have a reflection like this in the documentation somewhere as this is not the first time someone asks about it. That said, most studies who have used GGIR in the context of sedentary behaviour research then referred to their data as sedentary behaviour estimates.

A better solution would be to update the definition of sedentary behaviour to something that we can realistically measure and for which clearly defined gold standards exist.
See also my reflections on physical activity measurement, which suffers form the same poor construct definition: https://www.accelting.com/updates/how-to-measure-pa-guideline-adherence/

Best,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/
